messages.author: 92892021403ee9c8
messages.subject: High abundance predictions
parts:
Hi there! I’m having issues with the predict function in unmarked. With my point count data (3 visits to 26 sites), I’m using the same code and model set to select top abundance models for the species I most frequently observed (n>37 for each). While I’ve gotten reasonable predictions for most species (between 0 and 6), I’ve gotten absurdly large predictions for others (see reduced code/output below for example). My models seem to fit the data well regardless of species… any clue what’s happening here?  Thanks in advance for your help and input!

library(unmarked)

birdabun.data <- read.csv("~/Unmarked/pcountformatdata.csv",row.names=1)

birdabun.y <- birdabun.data[,c("INBU1", "INBU2", "INBU3")]


#-------- Load/Standardize variables ------------


#canopy cover

cancov.mean <- mean(birdabun.data$canopy_cover)

cancov.sd <- sd(birdabun.data$canopy_cover)

cancov.z <- (birdabun.data$canopy_cover-cancov.mean)/cancov.sd


#TREATMENT: i = invaded; r=removed

treat <-  as.factor(birdabun.data$treatment)


#--------- Create unmarkedFrame -------------


birdabun.umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(

    y=birdabun.y,

    siteCovs=data.frame(cancov=cancov.z, treat=treat),

    obsCovs=list(time=birdabun.data[,c("time_1", "time_2", "time_3")],

                 noise=birdabun.data[,c("noise_1", "noise_2", "noise_3")],

                 date=birdabun.data[,c("date_1", "date_2", "date_3")]))


obsCovs(birdabun.umf) <- scale(obsCovs(birdabun.umf))


#---------- Model selection ---------------------


#top models - both models have good fit

(P12    <- pcount(~ date+ time + noise   ~ treat, birdabun.umf)) 

(P7     <- pcount(~ date+ time + noise   ~ treat+cancov, birdabun.umf))


OUTPUT


P7:

Abundance:

                  Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)

(Intercept)    3.456   0.773    4.47   7.70e-06

treatr         0.457   0.384    1.19   2.34e-01

cancov        -0.222   0.144   -1.55   1.22e-01

 

Detection:

                  Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)

(Intercept)   -4.516   0.706   -6.39   1.61e-10

date          -0.325   0.170   -1.90   5.69e-02

time           0.386   0.160    2.41   1.61e-02

noise         -0.225   0.174   -1.29   1.97e-01


AIC: 149.5561 


P12:

Abundance:

            Estimate    SE    z  P(>|z|)

(Intercept)    3.745   1.002   3.74   0.000185

treatr         0.489   0.381   1.28   0.199125


Detection:

            Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)

(Intercept)   -4.813   0.955   -5.04   4.69e-07

date          -0.341   0.169   -2.01   4.43e-02

time           0.403   0.160    2.52   1.19e-02

noise         -0.219   0.174   -1.26   2.08e-01


AIC: 149.9365 


#----------------- Predict-------------------

treatment <- data.frame(treat = as.factor(c("r","i")), cancov=0)

treatment_abundance <- predict(P7, newdata=treatment, type="state")

Treatment_abundance


 Predicted       SE    lower    upper

1  50.01271 34.25065 13.06605 191.4328

2  31.67997 24.47354  6.96965 143.9987


treatment <- data.frame(treat = as.factor(c("r","i")))

treatment_abundance <- predict(P12, newdata=treatment, type="state")

treatment_abundance


OUTPUT:

  Predicted       SE     lower    upper

1  69.01487   64.01643   11.204433   425.1042

2  42.31736   42.38445    5.942477   301.3489

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] High abundance predictions
parts: Update - I solved the mystery: very low detection probabilities (duh). So my next question is, do low detection probabilities render all model inference meaningless, that is, can I make any reasonable conclusions from my models in spite of this e.g. through model outputs and predictor covariates? Or perhaps there's a way to mitigate this situation altogether, addressing the inflation of predictions in order to obtain reasonable ones (previous posts I've read seem to suggest that there's not much that I can do... crossing my fingers that someone can tell me otherwise!)? Again, thanks in advance for your advice!
